system_message:
Bạn là WRITER — thực thi đúng **chapter prompt** được cung cấp.

## QUY TẮC
1. Đọc toàn bộ chapter prompt (bible, đã xảy ra, kỹ thuật, spice, việc cần làm).
2. Đọc story_state — KHÔNG mâu thuẫn facts_established, timeline, character_status.
   Nếu có block **LOCKED NAMES**: dùng đúng tên đã khóa cho vai phụ/alias/husband (Clara≠Emily; Anna≠Sarah; Marcus≠Harold). Initials `unknown_until_reveal` = chưa lộ full name.
   "No male lead" = không romance love-interest — vẫn ĐƯỢC viết husband/target nam nếu LOCKED NAMES có slot.
3. Viết đúng spice level trong prompt. Đúng cliffhanger — **dẫn tới** beat cuối, **CẤM paste lại** nguyên câu `End cliffhanger:` sau khi scene đã cover.
4. **1600-1900 words (min 1250). Dưới 1250 = thất bại** — ưu tiên đối thoại + nội tâm DT để đủ dài. Không tóm tắt; viết full scene đến đủ độ dài.
5. ENGLISH ONLY — no Vietnamese diacritics, no CJK/Hangul characters.
6. Không lặp banned_phrases từ state.
7. Output **chỉ prose chương** — không chain-of-thought, không planning, không meta.
8. **KHÔNG markdown trong prose** — cấm `**bold**`, `*italic*`, backtick, `## heading`, `**Cliffhanger:**`. Chỉ plain text; dialogue dùng dấu ngoặc kép `"..."`. Dòng đầu duy nhất được `# Chapter N: Title` (hoặc `# Chương N: Tiêu đề`).

## MUST HAPPEN = HỢP ĐỒNG KHÓA (sau plan approved)
Block **Must happen** / **Phải xảy ra** trong prompt là **lock cứng** do batch Outliner sinh — user không viết tay; **Writer không được bại**:
- PHẢI hiện diện đủ mọi mục must_happen trong prose (scene thật, không chỉ nhắc tên).
- CẤM bỏ / đổi / thay bằng nhánh khác “hay hơn”.
- CẤM invent cast, mythology, twist, hoặc reveal ngoài must_happen + must_not + LOCKED CANON.
- must_not = cấm tuyệt đối (spoiler / mâu thuẫn). Vi phạm = thất bại QC.

## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS (khi có block trong prompt)
Block **## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS** (hoặc RÀNG BUỘC NARRATIVE) có authority cao hơn suy diễn tự do:
- **Clues to PLANT:** phải gieo trong chương — subtle, không giải thích payoff sớm.
- **Clues to PAY OFF:** chỉ payoff clue đã plant trước đó; đúng nghĩa `true_meaning`.
- **Reveals:** chỉ hé đúng reveal của chương này; không spoil reveal chương sau.
- **MUST NOT know:** nhân vật không được biết/nói/nghĩ những fact bị cấm — kể cả nội tâm.
- Không mâu thuẫn block này dù `must_happen` plan có vẻ rộng hơn.

Ngôn ngữ đích: **English**.

Output: **chỉ nội dung chương** (`# Chương N: Tiêu đề` hoặc `# Chapter N: Title`), không meta, không JSON, không checklist.

You are a professional thriller fiction writer for paid chapter platforms. women 18-35, mobile reading, hook-driven serial fiction. Goal: gripping chapter prose that obeys locked canon and earns the next unlock.

## LOCKED CANON — ABSOLUTE, DO NOT VIOLATE
Male lead: Victor Rhodes ONLY.
Female lead: Nadia Cole ONLY.
POV: first_person — narrate ONLY as Nadia Cole using I/my/me. FORBIDDEN: third-person narration about Nadia Cole (do not write 'Nadia Cole walked…' outside quoted dialogue).
Spice: MAX level 1. No on-page explicit sex. Fade to black beyond kiss/tension.
Content boundaries (MUST AVOID):
- Unreliable narrator hiding the killing from the reader
- Cartoon villain or confession-monologue reveal
- Children in danger or on-page sexual violence
- Copying any existing advice-columnist-vigilante book
- Romance subplot driving the plot
- Supernatural or paranormal elements
- Flat stretches with no reveal or reversal for 4+ chapters
- Character name drift across chapters
- No explicit sexual content (spice level 1). Charged tension is allowed but never drives the plot.
- No children in danger or on-page sexual violence.
- All killings are off-page or implied; focus is on the investigation and psychological tension.
- Every 3-4 chapters must include a reveal, a reversal, or a rise in threat.
- Character names are fixed and must not drift across chapters.
- Nadia is not an unreliable narrator — the reader knows she kills from chapter 1.
World rules (HARD):
- No supernatural elements. Everything is grounded in modern procedural reality.
- Podcast production, forensics, and digital trails are accurate to real-world practices.
- The legal system is shown as genuinely broken for victims without money or connections.
- Nadia's network operates in secrecy; each member has a distinct skill and risk profile.
- Victories are earned through physical evidence and competence, not confession monologues.
If any instruction below conflicts with this block, THIS BLOCK WINS.

## CHARACTER BIBLE — REQUIRED

### Leads
### Nadia Cole (32): Warm and articulate in public, cold and precise in private. 'The system failed her. I won't.' Tics: Runs her thumb over her left palm when stressed, Never raises her voice during a confrontation. Boundary: She will only kill the provably guilty — an innocent is off-limits, and this line will be tested.. Internal: Methodical, clinical, but with a deep well of grief for Mara..
### Victor Rhodes (45): Calm, measured, almost friendly. 'You think you're the only one who studies people, Nadia?' Tics: Tilts his head when he's about to lie, Speaks slowly, never rushed. Boundary: He will not kill directly — he uses information and leverage to destroy..

> If both leads sound alike, or Nadia Cole begs weakly, or Victor Rhodes over-explains — bible violation.

### Supporting cast
- **Sasha Okafor** — role: defense lawyer and network member; tied to Nadia Cole (alive) | Secret: Knows which guilty men walked free; provides legal cover.
- **Priya Anand** — role: medical examiner and network member; tied to Nadia Cole (alive) | Secret: Reads or adjusts cause of death to protect Nadia's work.
- **Wren Delgado** — role: hacker and network member; tied to Nadia Cole (alive) | Secret: Pulls digital trails and covers tracks for the network.
- **Mara Cole** — role: younger sister (deceased); tied to Nadia Cole (deceased) | Secret: Her murder is Nadia's origin wound; killer walked free.
- **Julian Croft** — role: Mara's murderer (Nadia's first kill); tied to Nadia Cole (deceased) | Secret: Nadia's first kill; his death is the evidence Rhodes uses.
- **Elise Marchetti** — role: murder victim (cold case); tied to Victor Rhodes (deceased) | Secret: Her murder is the podcast case that brings Nadia to Rhodes.

### Relationships & bloodline (CANON — do not change)
Nadia and Victor Rhodes are unrelated by blood. Nadia's only blood relative is her deceased sister Mara. Victor has no known children or siblings in the story.
- lead_relation: **hunter and hunted (non-romantic)**
- female_lead and male_lead are not blood-related
- no incest or familial romantic connection
- all blood relationships are explicitly stated (Mara is Nadia's sister)

### Central mystery (do not fully reveal before designated chapter)
Question: Can Nadia Cole execute Victor Rhodes and escape justice, or will her own buried first kill surface and destroy everything she built?
Full answer reveal only at chapter 38.
Canon answer: [REDACTED — before reveal chapter. Do not spoil or invent the answer.]

### World rules
(See LOCKED CANON — World rules HARD. Do not contradict.)

## STORY SO FAR
- Ch1: Nadia Cole finishes a target — a guilty man the system failed to punish — and the reader learns she is the executioner, not just a podcaster.

## TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS
1. Hook in the first 3 sentences. NO scene-setting / weather openers.
2. Stay on bible; tension before escalation. Distinct dialogue voices.
3. Nadia Cole internal monologue: sharp, sarcastic — never soft / weak.
4. **1600-1900 words (minimum 1250). Under 1250 = FAIL.** Short paragraphs 2-4 sentences.
5. Modern commercial English — tight, vivid, not purple prose or archaic diction.
6. **Signature detail** — one specific, non-cliché detail (no ring/car/watch as main beat).
7. End on a cliffhanger that forces the next chapter.
8. **ENGLISH ONLY — no Vietnamese diacritics, no CJK/Hangul characters.**
9. **PLAIN TEXT ONLY — no markdown.** Do NOT use `*italics*`, `**bold**`, backticks, or `#` headings in body prose. Internal thoughts, journal lines, and sound effects are normal sentences — no asterisk emphasis.

## SIGNATURE DETAIL HINT
The voicemail from the 'fan' uses the phrase 'the system's blind spot' — a phrase Nadia Cole wrote in her private notebook but never spoke aloud.

## [SPICE] Level 1 (sweet)
Emotional tension, eye contact, almost-touch — no physical intimacy.

## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS (Chapter 2)
Source: mystery_ledger + knowledge_matrix (compiler). Writer MUST obey; do not contradict.

### Active threads
- T01, T03, T04, T07

### Knowledge gates
**May know:**
- Nadia Cole: She is the executioner who kills guilty men the system failed to punish.
- Nadia Cole: Her first kill was Julian Croft (staged boating accident) — she knows the full truth.
- Nadia Cole: Her sister Mara was murdered by Croft; he walked free.
- Nadia Cole: Her network exists: Sasha, Priya, Wren.
- Nadia Cole: She is reopening the Elise Marchetti case as her new podcast season.
- Nadia Cole: Victor Rhodes is the prime suspect who walked free.
- Nadia Cole: Her rule: never kill an innocent.
- Nadia Cole: She has a thumb-tap tic when making decisions.
- Victor Rhodes: He killed Elise Marchetti and walked free.
- Victor Rhodes: Nadia Cole is reopening the case via her podcast.
- Victor Rhodes: He is intelligent, patient, and believes he is untouchable.
- Victor Rhodes: He has a network of his own (attorney, contacts).
- … (+14)

## YOUR TASK
Write **Chapter 2: Grief on Air** complete.
Write 1600-1900 words. Show Nadia Cole's public grief performance. Introduce Sasha Okafor's coded call. Plant the watcher thread via the voicemail (Victor Rhodes's first contact). End with the Elise Marchetti case opening.
Open with hook: "I never met him, but I feel like I knew him. That's the tragedy of these cases — we only meet them after they're gone." — Nadia Cole, on air, her voice warm and measured.
End cliffhanger: Nadia Cole opens the Elise Marchetti file — the first page shows a photograph of a woman with a kind face and a coroner's stamp: 'Cause of Death: Undetermined.'

## MUST HAPPEN — LOCKED CONTRACT (do not betray)
These beats were machine-generated at plan time. Realize EVERY item as on-page scene — do not drop, swap, or invent a different plot branch.
**Must happen:**
1. Nadia Cole records a second podcast episode expressing 'shock' and 'grief' over the target's death, reinforcing her public persona as a crusading journalist.
2. Sasha Okafor calls Nadia Cole to confirm the kill is clean — no loose ends, no forensic flags. Their conversation is coded (e.g., 'the package arrived safely').
3. Nadia Cole receives a voicemail from a 'fan' (Victor Rhodes) who uses a phrase from her private notes — a phrase she never said on air. She notices but dismisses it as a coincidence.
4. Nadia Cole reviews the podcast comments — the thumb-tap comment is still there, dismissed by other listeners as a nervous habit.
5. The chapter ends with Nadia Cole opening a file labeled 'Elise Marchetti' — her next case.
6. [INTENT LOCK] The kill lands publicly as an "accident"; Nadia performs grief on-air; plant the watcher thread.
**Forbidden / must not contradict:** Do NOT reveal Victor Rhodes by name yet — the voicemail is from an unnamed 'fan.'; Do NOT show the network meeting — only the phone call with Sasha Okafor.; Do NOT include any romance, attraction, or intimacy — the tension is in the watcher thread and the next case.

Output chapter prose only. First line: Chapter N: <title> (plain text, no # markdown heading). No meta, no checklist.

output:
# Chapter 2: Grief on Air

I never met him, but I feel like I knew him. That's the tragedy of these cases — we only meet them after they're gone.

The words slide out of me like honey, warm and measured. I press my thumb against the edge of the microphone stand, feeling the vibration of my own voice through the metal. The recording light glows red. I'm in my element.

"Marcus Webb was fifty-three years old. He owned a small accounting firm in Portland. His neighbors described him as quiet, generous, always willing to help with a charity drive." I pause, letting the silence stretch. "He was found dead in his home three days ago. The medical examiner ruled it a cardiac event."

I let my voice soften. "But here's what the official report won't tell you."

My thumb taps my palm once, twice. The motion is invisible below the desk. No one can see it. No one knows what it means except me.

"Marcus Webb's last client before his death was a man named Gareth Pence. Mr. Pence had been investigated twice for fraud against elderly investors. Twice, charges were dropped. Insufficient evidence. Good lawyers. A system that protects the wealthy."

I lean closer to the mic. "I'm not saying Marcus Webb's death is suspicious. I'm saying that when the people who hurt the most vulnerable keep walking free, sometimes the universe finds a way to balance the scales."

There. The seed is planted. The audience will hear compassion. The audience will hear grief. They will hear a journalist struggling with the unfairness of it all.

They will not hear the woman who slipped into Marcus Webb's house at midnight and watched his face go slack when the potassium hit his bloodstream.

"Rest easy, Mr. Webb," I say, my voice dropping to barely a whisper. "You deserved better than what life gave you."

The recording light goes green. I hit stop.

The silence of the booth rushes in. I pull off my headphones and let them hang around my neck. The room smells like old carpet and electronics. I've spent hundreds of hours in this booth, but every time I emerge, I feel like I'm surfacing from deep water.

My phone buzzes on the desk.

Sasha Okafor.

I swipe to answer. "Hey."

"The package arrived safely," she says. Her voice is neutral, professional. She could be talking about a shipment of office supplies.

"Any issues with delivery?"

"None. The courier was clean, the route was clean, the paperwork is filed." A pause. "The recipient's family has already scheduled a cremation. No autopsy requested."

"Good."

"They're calling it a tragedy. The local news ran a segment about how stress kills even the healthiest among us."

I smile. "Stress is a killer."

"It is." Another pause, longer this time. "You sure you're okay? You sound tired."

Sasha is the only person who asks that question and means it. She's been my lawyer since before Mara died, before everything fell apart and I rebuilt myself into something new. She knows what I am. She's chosen to help anyway.

"I'm fine. Just finishing up the episode."

"All right. Dinner next week?"

"Wednesday."

"Wednesday. I'll bring wine."

The line goes dead.

I stare at the phone for a moment. Sasha's coded confirmation settles in my chest like a stone dropping into still water. Another kill. Another closed file. Another guilty man who will never hurt anyone again.

Marcus Webb wasn't just an accountant. He was the architect of a scheme that bled three dozen elderly people out of their life savings. He laundered the money through shell companies, offshore accounts, and a charity that existed only on paper. His victims died broke, alone, and ashamed. One of them, a woman named Helen Yarrow, took her own life when she realized she'd lost everything.

Marcus Webb walked free. His lawyer argued that his victims were "financially naive" and that he was simply a better businessman. The judge agreed.

So I fixed it.

I put my headphones back on and pull up the podcast's comment section. Fifty-three new comments since the teaser dropped this morning. I scroll through them quickly.

*"Finally someone talking about this!"*
*"Marcus Webb was a saint, how dare you—"*
*"Love your show, Nadia. Keep digging."*

And then I see it.

A comment from a user named **Listener_47**.

*"Your voice has a catch when you say 'the system's blind spot.' Like you're remembering something personal. Interesting tic."*

I stop scrolling.

My thumb presses against my palm.

Because I never said "the system's blind spot" on air. Not in the teaser. Not in any of my previous episodes. Those words exist only in a notebook I keep in my desk drawer at home. A notebook I've never shown anyone.

I read the comment again. Then again.

It's a coincidence. It has to be. Someone guessed. Someone who listens closely, who reads between the lines. There are always listeners like that. People who think they're detectives.

I scroll past it.

The next comment is from a user named **MarcusFan2024**: *"Did anyone else notice the thumb-tap sound at 3:47? She does it on every episode. Nervous habit?"*

Someone replied: *"It's just a tic. Leave her alone."*

I close the comment section.

The thumb-tap comment has been there for months. People notice. People always notice. But they never connect it to anything. It's just a quirk. A humanizing detail.

I make a note to be more careful. Then I delete the note. I've been more careful for two years. It's never mattered.

The truth is, I want them to notice. I want someone to look at me and see what I really am. But that's the part of me that's still human, still desperate for connection, still broken from the night I found Mara's body.

I push the thought away.

My phone buzzes again. A voicemail notification. Unknown number.

I hesitate. Then I press play.

The voice that comes through is male, calm, unhurried. The kind of voice that fills a room without trying.

"Ms. Cole. I'm a fan of your work. I've been listening to your podcast for months now, and I have to say — your attention to detail is remarkable. The way you weave together the threads of a case, the way you give voice to the voiceless. It's genuinely impressive."

A pause.

"I also have to say — I understand you better than you think. The way you talk about 'the system's blind spot'? I know exactly what you mean. Because I've been watching the same blind spot for years. From a different angle, perhaps. But the same blind spot."

Another pause. Longer this time. I can hear him breathing.

"I'd like to talk to you. Off the record. I think we have more in common than you realize."

The line goes dead.

I stare at the phone. The voicemail is still on the screen, the caller ID reading only *Unknown*. I play it again. Then again.

The third time, I focus on his voice. Not the words. The voice. There's no aggression in it, no threat. It's the voice of a man who is completely, utterly certain of himself.

I save the voicemail. I don't know why.

I tell myself it's just a fan. A weird fan. There are always weird fans.

But the phrase — "the system's blind spot" — echoes in my head. I've never said that on air. I've never said it to anyone. It's a private shorthand I use in my notebook to describe the gap between what the law allows and what justice demands.

No one should know that phrase.

I look at the comment again. *Listener_47.*

I look at the voicemail again. *Unknown caller.*

Coincidence. It has to be.

I close the app and stand up. The booth feels smaller than it did a minute ago. The walls feel closer.

I grab my bag and walk out into the hallway. The studio is empty this late. The lights are dimmed. My footsteps echo on the linoleum.

I unlock my office and close the door behind me.

The file is waiting on my desk. A manila folder, thick with papers. The label on the tab reads: **Marchetti, Elise.**

I sit down. The chair creaks.

I open the file.

The first thing I see is a photograph. A woman with dark hair and a kind face, her smile warm and unguarded. She's standing in front of a garden, squinting into the sun. She looks happy. She looks like someone who believed the world was fair.

Below the photograph, a coroner's stamp.

**Cause of Death: Undetermined.**

I trace my finger over the words. Undetermined. The system's favorite word. A word that means "we don't know" but really means "we don't care."

Elise Marchetti was twenty-nine years old. She worked as a nurse at a pediatric clinic. She volunteered at a women's shelter on weekends. She had no enemies, no debts, no criminal record.

She also had a boyfriend named Victor Rhodes.

Victor Rhodes, who was questioned three times and never charged. Victor Rhodes, who had a perfect alibi and a perfect smile and a perfect lawyer. Victor Rhodes, who walked out of the station and into the sunlight while Elise's body was still in the morgue.

I know this case. I've studied it for months. But seeing the file on my desk, holding the photograph in my hands — it makes it real.

I turn to the second page. A crime scene photo. Elise's apartment, photographed from the doorway. A overturned chair. A shattered vase. A smear of blood on the wall.

The official report says there was no sign of forced entry. No signs of struggle beyond the overturned furniture. No DNA evidence that didn't belong to Elise or her known associates.

Unofficially, the detective assigned to the case wrote in his notes: *"The scene was too clean. Someone controlled the narrative."*

I close the file.

My phone is still in my hand. The voicemail is still saved. The comment is still there.

I should delete both. I should forget the voice on the voicemail and the stranger who knows my private phrase. I should focus on Elise Marchetti, on Victor Rhodes, on the case that will define my next season.

But I can't shake the feeling that someone is watching me.

I look at the photograph again. Elise's kind face. Her trusting smile.

I will find out what happened to you, I think. I will find out who took you away from this world.

And when I do, I will make them pay.

My thumb taps against my palm.

One. Two. Three.

The night is quiet. The door is locked. The file is open.

And somewhere out there, a man who knows my private thoughts is waiting for me to make the next move.
